Account.description:
An account's details. Never a secret, by construction.

`credential_stored` and `credential_ref` were being returned and were
absent from the hand-written type, so the screen could not tell a
configured account from one still waiting for its password.
Account.title: Account

ClientProblem.description: Something that went wrong in the desktop shell, not the backend.
ClientProblem.title: ClientProblem

CreatedTask.description:
What POST /tasks answers with, which is not a `Task`.

create_task() returns the five fields it just decided, and not `kind`
or `created_at`. The client typed this as a full Task, so two of its
fields were a fiction -- nothing reads them today, which is the only
reason it never bit.
CreatedTask.title: CreatedTask

FocusEnded.description: Ending a session answers with the one fact that changed.
FocusEnded.title: FocusEnded

FocusState.description:
One shape for GET /focus and POST /focus/start.

They returned two: the first carried `would_close` and not `message`,
the second the reverse. The Today screen stores the result of both in
the same state and reads `minutes_left` and `closed_apps` off either,
so the shapes were already required to agree and simply did not.
Making them one is the fix; the alternative is a client-side union
describing a difference with no reason behind it.
FocusState.title: FocusState

ParkedAction.description:
A pending action as /actions/pending lists it.

Not `PendingAction`: this one carries `expires_at` and that one does not,
and they were the same name on the wire until this file made the
difference visible. A confirmation has a TTL and a client that cannot see
it cannot tell a live question from a dead one.
ParkedAction.title: ParkedAction

PendingAction.description: An action waiting for a yes. The id is the whole contract (REQ-24).
PendingAction.title: PendingAction

ReferenceSaved.description: The clone status, plus what the upload itself produced.
ReferenceSaved.title: ReferenceSaved

RetentionWindow.description:
The window, and what is inside it right now (REQ-26).

Four fields, and the first draft of this model had five: an `oldest_turn`
that retention.describe() does not return and never has. Pydantic refused
the response and the endpoint answered 500, which is the right failure --
a response model that invents a field is a contract the server cannot
keep, and it is better to find that in a test than to have the field
quietly default itself into the schema.
RetentionWindow.title: RetentionWindow

SequenceRun.description:
What running a routine or a shortcut did, per step.

`routine_id` duplicates `id` and is kept: it is the name routines used
before shortcuts existed, and dropping it from the schema would be a
breaking change dressed up as tidying.
SequenceRun.title: SequenceRun

SkillCall.description:
One gate outcome, as GateOutcome.to_dict() produces it.

The hand-written TypeScript described three of these eight fields. That
was not wrong -- TypeScript does not object to fields it was not told
about -- but it meant `data` and `action_id` were being used from the
wire with no type behind them.
SkillCall.title: SkillCall

SkillEntry.description: One catalog entry, as the router sees it.
SkillEntry.title: SkillEntry

StageMedians.description:
Medians over the window. Zeroes when it is empty, which is honest for a
median of nothing and saves the panel a null check per field.
StageMedians.title: StageMedians

StoppedCapture.description:
A finished recording, with the summary this call just produced.

Not a subclass of `Transcript`: that one's `summary` is whatever was
stored and so is open-ended, and narrowing a field in a subclass is a
promise the parent did not make. Here the shape *is* known, because
summarize.summarise() produced it one line above -- so it is spelled out,
and the duplication is the price of the two being genuinely different.
StoppedCapture.title: StoppedCapture

TimingSummary.description:
What /diagnostics/timings answers (REQ-27).

`turns` is newest first and at most `capacity` long -- a ring in memory,
never written down. The medians and the slowest turn are computed in
app/timings.py rather than in the UI, so the CLI can ask the same question
and get the same number.
TimingSummary.title: TimingSummary

TurnTiming.description: One turn's milliseconds, as timings.TurnTiming.to_dict() produces it.
TurnTiming.title: TurnTiming

get.description:
Whether the avatar's runtime may load.

Says nothing about whether the Core file is actually present: it is a
front-end asset compiled into the desktop binary, which this process cannot
see. The window checks for it directly and reports that itself.

post.description:
Record — or withdraw — acceptance of the Live2D runtime licence.

Stamped with the date so the record can be shown back rather than asserted.
Withdrawing clears the date too: keeping "accepted on the 3rd" next to
"accepted: false" is a config that contradicts itself.

Logged at WARNING like the egress switches. This is not a privacy decision,
but it is a legal one made on this machine, and the point of writing it down
is that it can be found later.

get.description: Account details only. Never returns a secret, by construction.

post.description:
Add an account without hand-editing YAML (REQ-13, REQ-26).

Details only. No password crosses this boundary — `fields` is rejected
outright if it carries anything that looks like one, and the response says
to run `/connect`, which prompts at the terminal and writes to the OS
credential store.

Try the account and say whether it works.

Without this, a wrong password is discovered the next time the user asks
about their mail, as an error about something they were not doing.

put.description:
Store the password (or an iCal URL) for an account — REQ-26.

This used to be terminal-only, on the reasoning that a secret typed into a
form travels through a request body and a validation layer before it reaches
anywhere safe, whereas one typed at a getpass prompt goes straight from the
keyboard to the OS store. That reasoning is sound and was still the wrong
call: an assistant whose accounts can only be set up by running commands in
a terminal is not configurable by the people it is for, and "secure but
unused" is not secure.

So the secret crosses one loopback hop, and everything else is held tight
around it. The API binds 127.0.0.1 only and CORS is an allow-list, so no
page on the internet can reach this. The value is not logged here or in
credentials.store, is never returned by any endpoint, and never touches
kai.config.yaml. What lands on disk is a reference.

post.description:
Record a failure the frontend hit — REQ-27.

The window can reach things the backend cannot: the updater, the WebView,
the Live2D runtime. When one of those fails, the only account of it was a
sentence in a card that disappears when the user clicks elsewhere, and the
console it was also written to needs devtools that a packaged build does
not ship.

That is not a hypothetical gap. An update failed on a real install and the
whole investigation came down to asking the user to read the message back,
because nothing had kept it. A failure nobody can retrieve ten minutes
later cannot be diagnosed, only guessed at.

Logged, never stored in the database: it is a line in the same file
/diagnostics/logs points at, and it goes through the same Redactor as
everything else there.

get.description:
Where the log is and how big it is — REQ-27.

Names and sizes, never contents. A log is a file to attach to a bug report,
not something to render in a chat window, and serving the text would put a
second copy somewhere it was not already.

How long recent turns took, by stage — REQ-27.

Beside /diagnostics/logs because it answers the other half of the same
question, and with the same restraint: the log says how big it is and not
what is in it, and this says how long a turn took and not what was asked.
Six numbers per turn, the last fifty turns, in memory only -- see
app/timings.py for why none of it is written down.

delete.description: REQ-16/REQ-26 — the user can see what is indexed and remove all of it.

get.description:
Whether meaning-based search is on, and how much of the index has it.

"Semantic search is enabled" is not a useful claim on its own: the setting
can be on, the model absent, and every query still purely lexical. So the
answer carries the model, whether it is actually pulled, and the count.

post.description:
Pull the embedding model. Explicit, and never on startup.

274MB, which is small next to the language model already required but is
still hundreds of megabytes that must not move because somebody opened
Settings. Same rule the voice models follow.

get.description:
Everything the shell used to poll for, pushed instead — REQ-31, REQ-32.

Presence, notifications and brain health arrived through three timers
running for the life of the window: roughly 48 requests a minute with the
app idle, to establish forty-seven times out of forty-eight that nothing had
changed. See app/events.py for what is sampled and how often.

/state and /notifications stay. The CLI uses them, they are what this is
tested against, and an endpoint that answers one question once is the right
shape for a script.

Focus state, plus what starting one would cost right now.

`would_close` is the whole reason this is not just a button. Starting a
session terminates the configured distracting apps, and unsaved work in them
is gone. The skill decides its severity the same way -- consequential only
when something is actually running -- so the UI can name the apps before
asking instead of warning about a risk that does not exist today.
Drain queued notifications. Destructive: each is handed out once.

post.description:
Everything the database holds about you, as one zip — REQ-26.

The counterpart to /privacy/wipe, and the reason it needed one: until now
the only control over the record was destroying it. REQ-26 asks for local
data *control*, and a switch that only points one way is not a dial.

No secrets, by construction: `credentials.fetch` is never called, and the
connectors section is removed from the exported config rather than emptied,
so there is no field left to wonder about. app/privacy_export.py lists what
else is left out and why.

Written to a file and streamed rather than assembled in memory. Transcripts
are the one table with no bound on their size, so an endpoint that holds
the whole export in RAM to hand it over is one that fails on exactly the
install that most wants it.

The temporary file is deleted after the response is sent, which is what
BackgroundTasks is for -- deleting it before would race the download, and
leaving it would put a second copy of everything in the data directory
under a button about data control.

get.description:
What an export would hold, without building one.

So the button can say "4 facts, 112 turns, 3 meetings" before it is
pressed. Offering a download of an unknown thing is how people end up not
pressing it.
The window, and what is inside it right now — REQ-26.

post.description:
Apply the window now rather than waiting for the next start or stop.

Here because shortening the window should visibly do something. Saving "30
days" and being told nothing happened until the next restart reads as a
setting that did not take.
REQ-26 — the single delete-everything action.

Deliver anything due right now. Used by tests and by the UI on wake.

Waits for any routine the tick queued. Routines run on their own worker so
a slow one cannot hold up reminder delivery or the indexer -- but this
endpoint exists to make the due thing happen while somebody is looking at
it, so returning before the routine has run would report a tick that had
only been scheduled.

Re-approve a routine whose steps changed — REQ-12, REQ-24.

The other half of "re-prompt if the routine is later edited". Editing
revokes the approval; this is where the user gives it again, having seen the
steps listed on the screen that offers this button.
Run a routine now. Useful for checking one does what you meant.

patch.description:
Change a setting (REQ-26).

What may be changed is `preferences.WRITABLE` and nothing else — a section
or key absent from it is a 403 whatever the caller asks for. `connectors.*`
is absent because those carry secrets and go through
/connectors/accounts, and `brain.ollama_host` is absent because redirecting
the model host would send every prompt somewhere else.

Egress switches and folder lists *are* writable, which they were not
before. Folder lists are validated against the filesystem, and every egress
change is logged with its previous value, so widening what the assistant can
reach leaves a record even though it no longer needs a text editor.

post.description: Re-approve a shortcut whose steps changed — REQ-22, REQ-24.
Direct invocation, still through the gate — there is no bypass.

get.description:
What the presence indicator shows — REQ-32.

Deliberately the whole contract: a state name, plus an optional emotion tag.
The UI is given nothing about the brain, the skills or the actions, which is
what keeps the presentation layer replaceable.

post.description:
The same turn, delivered as it happens (REQ-27, REQ-32).

Server-sent events rather than a WebSocket: this is one-way, short-lived,
and survives a dropped connection by simply ending. A socket would add a
lifecycle to manage for no capability the turn needs.

Every event is one `data:` line of JSON with a `type`:

    stage  - which slow phase is running, so the UI can say so
    delta  - a piece of the reply
    done   - the finished TurnResult, identical to what POST /turn returns

`done` always arrives, including on failure, and its reply is the
authoritative text: receipts and the ungrounded-answer guard can both revise
what the deltas already showed, so a client renders deltas as they come and
then settles on `done`.

Record — or withdraw — the acknowledgement that gates cloning.

Withdrawing switches the engine back to Piper in the same call. Leaving
`tts_engine: xtts` set while consent is false would mean the setting said
one thing and the behaviour did another; tts.use_cloned_voice() would refuse
anyway, but a config that lies about what it is doing is its own problem.

delete.description: Give the disk space back. As easy as spending it.

post.description:
Start fetching the cloning engine. Explicit, and never on startup.

Returns immediately rather than holding the request open for a download
measured in hundreds of megabytes: the settings screen polls the GET above.
A second call while one is running is refused by the installer's own lock
rather than starting a competing download.

Record — or withdraw — acceptance of XTTS-v2's licence.

Kept separate from `clone_consent` on purpose. That switch is about the
ethics of copying somebody's voice; this is agreeing to a non-commercial
software licence. They are different questions with different answers, and
one switch meaning both would be an acceptance nobody was shown.

Withdrawing clears the date, for the same reason the Live2D gate does: a
config reading "not accepted, accepted on the 3rd" contradicts itself.

delete.description: Delete the recording. It is a sample of somebody's voice (REQ-26).

post.description:
Take the reference sample as an uploaded audio file.

This replaced recording from the microphone. The argument for recording was
that it put whoever is being cloned in the room -- but it is not enforcement
(a phone held to a laptop defeats it) and it made the feature unusable for
the ordinary case of already having a clean recording of your own voice.
Since it bought manners rather than safety, the consent acknowledgement is
doing the real work, and this is the more useful shape.

Anything ffmpeg-free is accepted directly: WAV in, PCM out. Other formats
are refused by name rather than half-decoded into noise that only reveals
itself when the clone speaks.
Capture one utterance and run it as a normal turn.
Explicit download. Hundreds of MB never move without being asked for.

Say something out loud, and describe its shape for the avatar.

This used to call synthesize() and return the duration -- rendering the
audio and discarding it. The CLI and the voice loop both call tts.speak(),
which plays; this endpoint did not, so the desktop app's "speak replies
aloud" switch produced silence while every other path worked.

Playback is non-blocking so the response comes back at the moment sound
starts rather than when it finishes. That matters for the avatar: the
envelope below is walked from the moment this returns, so a blocking call
would put the mouth a whole sentence behind the voice.
